title: Room-temperature high-efficiency spin injection via van der Waals tunnel contact

paper_content.abstract: Efficient and reliable spin injection at room temperature with scalability is crucial for spintronic applications but remains challenging. Direct ferromagnetic metal deposition on two-dimensional materials often leads to inefficient transparent contacts. Here, we introduce an indium buffer layer between ferromagnetic cobalt (Co) and graphene to establish high-efficiency van der Waals (vdW) tunnel contacts. This buffer layer facilitates a physisorption interface between Co and graphene with a well-defined vdW gap, which functions as an effective spin tunnel barrier. Through buffer layer thickness optimization, we achieved a room-temperature spin injection efficiency of approximately 25% in graphene, comparable to the best single-crystalline oxide-tunnel-barrier-based devices, alongside explicit nonlocal spin valve signals and Hanle spin precession. We further demonstrate the scalability of our approach through uniform performance across multi-channel graphene spin valves and its versatility by achieving efficient spin injection in semiconducting MoS2 with an average efficiency of about 19.7%. Our strategy offers a simple, cost-efficient, and industry-compatible method for future large-scale and efficient spintronic applications.
paper_content.introduction:
Graphene has emerged as an ideal spin transport platform due to its extremely small spin-orbital coupling, negligible hyperfine interaction as well as ultra-high charge mobility1–3. Electrical spin injection by direct deposition of ferromagnetic (FM) metal on graphene mostly forms a transparent contact with small contact resistance, which results in extremely low spin injection efficiency4,5. To maximize the potential of graphene for spintronic applications, various dielectric materials, such as metal oxides and van der Waals (vdW) hexagonal boron nitride (hBN)6–11, have been exploited and inserted between the FM electrode and graphene to form a tunnel contact in order to improve the injection efficiency12–14. In fact, the growth of a uniform oxide barrier is non-trivial and ubiquitous pinholes form due to high surface diffusivity on the dangling-bond-free graphene surface. By using TiO2 as a seed layer, an atomically smooth MgO barrier has been grown on graphene, so far with the widely accepted highest spin injection efficiency of 26–30%15. However, reaching such high efficiency relies on complex and delicate growth control based on ultra-high vacuum molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) technique, which hinders its widespread applications. Two-dimensional (2D) vdW hBN has been predicted as an ideal pinhole-free tunnel barrier16. Nevertheless, the precise control of its layer thickness and avoidance of transfer-process-induced contamination and bubbles/wrinkles are challenging, making the reported efficiency vary widely from device to device17–21.

A promising way to achieve reliable spin injection with simple processing is based on dielectric-barrier-free vdW contact between FM electrode and graphene, where naturally formed vdW gap serves as the tunnel barrier22,23. Recent studies using transfer techniques to stack 2D ferromagnet on graphene to form vdW contacts have claimed successful spin injection, but most without the explicit proof of Hanle precession signal24–27. Moreover, the efficiency remains low and scalability has yet to be addressed, as large-scale growth and transfer of 2D ferromagnets are immature. To advance toward scalable applications, making vdW contact based on three-dimensional (3D) FM metal instead of 2D ferromagnet is more promising28,29. Yet, directly evaporating 3D FM metal on 2D materials hardly forms vdW contact. Theoretical calculations have shown that FM metal, such as cobalt (Co), generates a strongly hybridized chemisorption interface when adsorbed on graphene, being the reason for forming a transparent contact with a negligible barrier and extremely small contact resistance30,31. A viable solution is to insert a buffer metal layer, which forms a physisorption interface with graphene, before depositing the FM metal layer so as to mitigate their direct hybridization. Inspiring results have been shown32,33, whereas, unambiguous demonstration of room-temperature spin injection via combinational observation of nonlocal spin valve signal and Hanle spin precession as well as achieving high spin injection efficiency, has yet to be realized.

In this work, by growing an indium (In) buffer layer between ferromagnetic Co electrode and graphene, we show that vdW contact with a gap of ~2.83 Å and an effective tunnel barrier height of ~62.8 meV has been successfully established. Analysis based on a one-dimensional drift-diffusion model of spin transport further corroborates the vdW-gap-mediated efficient spin tunnelling and transport in our Co/In-contacted devices. Both the nonlocal spin valve signal and Hanle spin precession have been explicitly observed at room temperature, which unambiguously proves successful spin injection via the vdW tunnel contact. Upon optimizing the In buffer layer thickness and gate control, a spin injection efficiency of ~25% at room temperature and ~35% at low temperature has been achieved, comparable to the best values reported in oxide-tunnel-barrier-based graphene lateral spin vales (LSV). By making a multi-channel LSV device on an ultra-long graphene sample, both high device yield and performance uniformity were demonstrated, further supporting the scalability of our approach. Finally, we show that our strategy is readily applicable to other 2D materials such as semiconducting MoS2, where an efficiency as high as ~19.7% was obtained.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors made a substantial effort to answer all the questions raised by the 4 reviewers, which were properly answered in most cases. However, I still have some concerns about the spin injection in MoS2: the authors show the Hanle precession, but it is not clear if the data reported is the subtraction of parallel and antiparallel configuration or simply the parallel case. They should provide the 2 curves (parallel and antiparallel) as they do for graphene, otherwise a simple Lorentzian curve with magnetic field like the one shown could arise from some magnetoresistance effect like weak localization in the channel.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Dear Editor,
Please find below my comments on the responses provided by the authors of the paper entitled “Room-temperature high-efficiency spin injection via van der Waals tunnel contact”, regarding my comments for the revue in Nature Electronics Journal.
The authors present a methodical study, from sample fabrication to physical characterization and spin-dependent transport in multi-terminal lateral spin-valves (LSV), and report and focus on the performance of the spin injection into 2D materials (graphene and MoS2) using a Co/In polarizing electrode. I would like to thank the authors for the responses and the additional information and new experiments they have performed and included in the manuscript. Nevertheless, I still have main reserves concerning the novelty of the results the authors provide on graphene based LSV. However, the improved work carried out on MoS2-LSV deserves to be highlighted.
The authors have now discussed the pivotal point regarding the spin injection efficiency, namely the impedance mismatch issue with measures and calculations. The authors provide the calculated two-terminal resistance, from electrical measurements and geometrical parameters. The contact resistance is included in a range from “100 ~ 300 kΩ” which is as mentioned by the authors “comparable to that reported in the MBE-grown pinhole-free Co/MgO/graphene tunnel contacts”, I agree. The authors then extract the spin polarization of Co/In electrode using the Takahashi and Maek’s formula (S. Takahashi and S. Maekawa, Spin injection and detection in magnetic nanostructures. Phys. Rev. B 67, 052409 (2003)) by implementing all the parameters of the device, including the non-local resistivity measured in the Co/In/graphene in two-terminal configuration. They obtain a spin efficiency of 25%. Nevertheless, this value which I note, remains “comparable to the best values reported in oxide-tunnel-barrier based graphene lateral spin valve”, as claimed by the authors (Han, W. et al. Tunneling Spin Injection into Single Layer Graphene. Phys. Rev. Lett., 105, 167202 (2010)). Authors provide sketch for two-terminal non-local measurements. I still have fundamental concern on the multi-LSV geometry. When spin is injected into the graphene channel, even if the detection is monitored between two terminals, all others electrodes are electrically connected with the graphene channel. Therefore, if the contact resistance of the Co/In electrode which detects the spin signal in the two-terminal configuration is too high compared to another distant electrode connected on graphene, then this distant electrode acts as a spin well. The effective spin signal drops, and it does not allow determine the full picture, i.e value, of the spin polarization of the electrode to be assessed because not all of the signal is detected (Seneor et al., Spintronics with graphene, MRS Bulletin 37, 1245 (2012)). In summary, without considering recent publication form Sarkar et al., Nat. Electron. 8, 215–221 (2025), which report on results on a Co/In/graphene-based LSV and about which I would have had the same doubts regarding its novelty in light of the work reported in recent years on graphene-based spintronics LSV (Stephan Roche et al. 2015 2D Mater. 2 030202), I do not recommend the article for publication in Nature Communications.
In contrast, the authors have strengthened their argument by providing new data and measurements on MoS2-LSV study. The field of research of TMDCs based spintronics, as MoS2, is fairly recent and deserves further exploration. With this new augmented dataset (STEM of Co/In/MoS2, spin-dependent transport on several samples comforting the reproducibility of authors’ previous measurements, extraction of a 20% spin polarization), the study deserves a new perspective. I encourage the authors to rethink the article and focus it on MoS2 results, which is of interest to the community and further benefit the field.

Response: Thank you very much for reviewing our work once again. We highly appreciate your positive comments on the MoS -LSV part of the work. However, as to the graphene-based LSV part, 2 we believe the importance and advance of our work have NOT been fully recognized and appreciated.

Response: It seems your main argument against the novelty of our work is that we only claim comparable spin injection efficiency with the best value reported in oxide-tunnel-barrier based graphene lateral spin valve, but not higher. We have the following responses:
Firstly, it should be emphasized that the best spin injection efficiency value reported by Han, W. et al. [1] was based on MBE-grown single-crystalline MgO tunnel barrier, where the growth process was complex and the UHV-condition is highly demanding, making it cost-inefficient and unfavorable for scaling up. By contrast, the follow-up work using sputtered MgO barriers (polycrystalline or non-crystalline) typically exhibited low spin injection efficiency of only ~ 5% [8].
Secondly, there is a misunderstanding of the key points of our work, where the high spin injection efficiency is NOT the only claim. To sum up, the key novelty and advance of our work as compared to previous graphene-based spintronics work is actually that we have developed an effective 3D vdW contact strategy which offers a combination of advantages over all the previous methods on spin injection efficiency, process simplicity, repeatability, scalability and CMOS-compatibility, as comparatively shown in the table below. As you can see, in view of all the five key aspects that determine the practical application potential, our strategy all stands out.

Response: We do NOT think our explanation of the multi-LSV geometry measurement has been properly understood. So, let’s elucidate the measurement mechanism once again based on the schematics shown below, where Fig. a shows the case without “spin sink” (“spin well” as you name) effect and Fig. b shows the case with “spin sink” effect.
The so-called spin signal is the nonlocal voltage drop (V , for parallel configuration) measured p between detector electrode and reference electrode as shown in Fig. a. Because we always use the outermost electrode as reference, where the spin chemical potential is close to zero (due to long distance diffusion), so V is nearly solely determined by the spin chemical potential at the detector p electrode. Note that monolayer graphene is an absolute 2D system, so there should be NO shorting problem across the detector electrode (i.e. no current can “bypass” it; if otherwise the channel material has finite thickness instead, then current may “bypass” the electrode by flowing through the bottom side of the channel to the sink electrode), namely all spins injected at the injector electrode must diffuse to the detector electrode first, then pass it, and diffuse to remote electrodes. When there is a “spin sink” electrode between detector electrode and reference electrode as shown in Fig. b, the spin chemical potential will quickly drop to zero at this electrode before reaching the reference electrode. However, this doesn’t affect the spin chemical potential detected at the detector electrode at all, so V remains almost unaffected. In the worst case, for somehow if “not all of the p signal is detected” as you assumed, then V should be underestimated NOT overestimated, which p means that the spin injection efficiency we extracted actually sets the lower bound of the real value.

Response: It’s a regret that you may have underrated the potential impact Sarkar’s work and our work could bring to this field. ## Abstract

Efficient and reliable spin injection at room temperature with scalability is crucial for spintronic applications but remains challenging. Direct ferromagnetic metal deposition on two-dimensional materials often leads to inefficient transparent contacts. Here, we introduce an indium buffer layer between ferromagnetic cobalt (Co) and graphene to establish high-efficiency van der Waals (vdW) tunnel contacts. This buffer layer facilitates a physisorption interface between Co and graphene with a well-defined vdW gap, which functions as an effective spin tunnel barrier. Through buffer layer thickness optimization, we achieved a room-temperature spin injection efficiency of approximately 25% in graphene, comparable to the best single-crystalline oxide-tunnel-barrier-based devices, alongside explicit nonlocal spin valve signals and Hanle spin precession. We further demonstrate the scalability of our approach through uniform performance across multi-channel graphene spin valves and its versatility by achieving efficient spin injection in semiconducting MoS2 with an average efficiency of about 19.7%. Our strategy offers a simple, cost-efficient, and industry-compatible method for future large-scale and efficient spintronic applications.

---

## Introduction

Graphene has emerged as an ideal spin transport platform due to its extremely small spin-orbital coupling, negligible hyperfine interaction as well as ultra-high charge mobility1–3. Electrical spin injection by direct deposition of ferromagnetic (FM) metal on graphene mostly forms a transparent contact with small contact resistance, which results in extremely low spin injection efficiency4,5. To maximize the potential of graphene for spintronic applications, various dielectric materials, such as metal oxides and van der Waals (vdW) hexagonal boron nitride (hBN)6–11, have been exploited and inserted between the FM electrode and graphene to form a tunnel contact in order to improve the injection efficiency12–14. In fact, the growth of a uniform oxide barrier is non-trivial and ubiquitous pinholes form due to high surface diffusivity on the dangling-bond-free graphene surface. By using TiO2 as a seed layer, an atomically smooth MgO barrier has been grown on graphene, so far with the widely accepted highest spin injection efficiency of 26–30%15. However, reaching such high efficiency relies on complex and delicate growth control based on ultra-high vacuum molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) technique, which hinders its widespread applications. Two-dimensional (2D) vdW hBN has been predicted as an ideal pinhole-free tunnel barrier16. Nevertheless, the precise control of its layer thickness and avoidance of transfer-process-induced contamination and bubbles/wrinkles are challenging, making the reported efficiency vary widely from device to device17–21.

A promising way to achieve reliable spin injection with simple processing is based on dielectric-barrier-free vdW contact between FM electrode and graphene, where naturally formed vdW gap serves as the tunnel barrier22,23. Recent studies using transfer techniques to stack 2D ferromagnet on graphene to form vdW contacts have claimed successful spin injection, but most without the explicit proof of Hanle precession signal24–27. Moreover, the efficiency remains low and scalability has yet to be addressed, as large-scale growth and transfer of 2D ferromagnets are immature. To advance toward scalable applications, making vdW contact based on three-dimensional (3D) FM metal instead of 2D ferromagnet is more promising28,29. Yet, directly evaporating 3D FM metal on 2D materials hardly forms vdW contact. Theoretical calculations have shown that FM metal, such as cobalt (Co), generates a strongly hybridized chemisorption interface when adsorbed on graphene, being the reason for forming a transparent contact with a negligible barrier and extremely small contact resistance30,31. A viable solution is to insert a buffer metal layer, which forms a physisorption interface with graphene, before depositing the FM metal layer so as to mitigate their direct hybridization. Inspiring results have been shown32,33, whereas, unambiguous demonstration of room-temperature spin injection via combinational observation of nonlocal spin valve signal and Hanle spin precession as well as achieving high spin injection efficiency, has yet to be realized.

In this work, by growing an indium (In) buffer layer between ferromagnetic Co electrode and graphene, we show that vdW contact with a gap of ~2.83 Å and an effective tunnel barrier height of ~62.8 meV has been successfully established. Analysis based on a one-dimensional drift-diffusion model of spin transport further corroborates the vdW-gap-mediated efficient spin tunnelling and transport in our Co/In-contacted devices. Both the nonlocal spin valve signal and Hanle spin precession have been explicitly observed at room temperature, which unambiguously proves successful spin injection via the vdW tunnel contact. Upon optimizing the In buffer layer thickness and gate control, a spin injection efficiency of ~25% at room temperature and ~35% at low temperature has been achieved, comparable to the best values reported in oxide-tunnel-barrier-based graphene lateral spin vales (LSV). By making a multi-channel LSV device on an ultra-long graphene sample, both high device yield and performance uniformity were demonstrated, further supporting the scalability of our approach. Finally, we show that our strategy is readily applicable to other 2D materials such as semiconducting MoS2, where an efficiency as high as ~19.7% was obtained.

## Paper

## Abstract

Efficient and reliable spin injection at room temperature with scalability is crucial for spintronic applications but remains challenging. Direct ferromagnetic metal deposition on two-dimensional materials often leads to inefficient transparent contacts. Here, we introduce an indium buffer layer between ferromagnetic cobalt (Co) and graphene to establish high-efficiency van der Waals (vdW) tunnel contacts. This buffer layer facilitates a physisorption interface between Co and graphene with a well-defined vdW gap, which functions as an effective spin tunnel barrier. Through buffer layer thickness optimization, we achieved a room-temperature spin injection efficiency of approximately 25% in graphene, comparable to the best single-crystalline oxide-tunnel-barrier-based devices, alongside explicit nonlocal spin valve signals and Hanle spin precession. We further demonstrate the scalability of our approach through uniform performance across multi-channel graphene spin valves and its versatility by achieving efficient spin injection in semiconducting MoS2 with an average efficiency of about 19.7%. Our strategy offers a simple, cost-efficient, and industry-compatible method for future large-scale and efficient spintronic applications.

---

## Introduction

Graphene has emerged as an ideal spin transport platform due to its extremely small spin-orbital coupling, negligible hyperfine interaction as well as ultra-high charge mobility1–3. Electrical spin injection by direct deposition of ferromagnetic (FM) metal on graphene mostly forms a transparent contact with small contact resistance, which results in extremely low spin injection efficiency4,5. To maximize the potential of graphene for spintronic applications, various dielectric materials, such as metal oxides and van der Waals (vdW) hexagonal boron nitride (hBN)6–11, have been exploited and inserted between the FM electrode and graphene to form a tunnel contact in order to improve the injection efficiency12–14. In fact, the growth of a uniform oxide barrier is non-trivial and ubiquitous pinholes form due to high surface diffusivity on the dangling-bond-free graphene surface. By using TiO2 as a seed layer, an atomically smooth MgO barrier has been grown on graphene, so far with the widely accepted highest spin injection efficiency of 26–30%15. However, reaching such high efficiency relies on complex and delicate growth control based on ultra-high vacuum molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) technique, which hinders its widespread applications. Two-dimensional (2D) vdW hBN has been predicted as an ideal pinhole-free tunnel barrier16. Nevertheless, the precise control of its layer thickness and avoidance of transfer-process-induced contamination and bubbles/wrinkles are challenging, making the reported efficiency vary widely from device to device17–21.

A promising way to achieve reliable spin injection with simple processing is based on dielectric-barrier-free vdW contact between FM electrode and graphene, where naturally formed vdW gap serves as the tunnel barrier22,23. Recent studies using transfer techniques to stack 2D ferromagnet on graphene to form vdW contacts have claimed successful spin injection, but most without the explicit proof of Hanle precession signal24–27. Moreover, the efficiency remains low and scalability has yet to be addressed, as large-scale growth and transfer of 2D ferromagnets are immature. To advance toward scalable applications, making vdW contact based on three-dimensional (3D) FM metal instead of 2D ferromagnet is more promising28,29. Yet, directly evaporating 3D FM metal on 2D materials hardly forms vdW contact. Theoretical calculations have shown that FM metal, such as cobalt (Co), generates a strongly hybridized chemisorption interface when adsorbed on graphene, being the reason for forming a transparent contact with a negligible barrier and extremely small contact resistance30,31. A viable solution is to insert a buffer metal layer, which forms a physisorption interface with graphene, before depositing the FM metal layer so as to mitigate their direct hybridization. Inspiring results have been shown32,33, whereas, unambiguous demonstration of room-temperature spin injection via combinational observation of nonlocal spin valve signal and Hanle spin precession as well as achieving high spin injection efficiency, has yet to be realized.

In this work, by growing an indium (In) buffer layer between ferromagnetic Co electrode and graphene, we show that vdW contact with a gap of ~2.83 Å and an effective tunnel barrier height of ~62.8 meV has been successfully established. Analysis based on a one-dimensional drift-diffusion model of spin transport further corroborates the vdW-gap-mediated efficient spin tunnelling and transport in our Co/In-contacted devices. Both the nonlocal spin valve signal and Hanle spin precession have been explicitly observed at room temperature, which unambiguously proves successful spin injection via the vdW tunnel contact. Upon optimizing the In buffer layer thickness and gate control, a spin injection efficiency of ~25% at room temperature and ~35% at low temperature has been achieved, comparable to the best values reported in oxide-tunnel-barrier-based graphene lateral spin vales (LSV). By making a multi-channel LSV device on an ultra-long graphene sample, both high device yield and performance uniformity were demonstrated, further supporting the scalability of our approach. Finally, we show that our strategy is readily applicable to other 2D materials such as semiconducting MoS2, where an efficiency as high as ~19.7% was obtained.

## Paper

## Abstract

Efficient and reliable spin injection at room temperature with scalability is crucial for spintronic applications but remains challenging. Direct ferromagnetic metal deposition on two-dimensional materials often leads to inefficient transparent contacts. Here, we introduce an indium buffer layer between ferromagnetic cobalt (Co) and graphene to establish high-efficiency van der Waals (vdW) tunnel contacts. This buffer layer facilitates a physisorption interface between Co and graphene with a well-defined vdW gap, which functions as an effective spin tunnel barrier. Through buffer layer thickness optimization, we achieved a room-temperature spin injection efficiency of approximately 25% in graphene, comparable to the best single-crystalline oxide-tunnel-barrier-based devices, alongside explicit nonlocal spin valve signals and Hanle spin precession. We further demonstrate the scalability of our approach through uniform performance across multi-channel graphene spin valves and its versatility by achieving efficient spin injection in semiconducting MoS2 with an average efficiency of about 19.7%. Our strategy offers a simple, cost-efficient, and industry-compatible method for future large-scale and efficient spintronic applications.

---

## Introduction

Graphene has emerged as an ideal spin transport platform due to its extremely small spin-orbital coupling, negligible hyperfine interaction as well as ultra-high charge mobility1–3. Electrical spin injection by direct deposition of ferromagnetic (FM) metal on graphene mostly forms a transparent contact with small contact resistance, which results in extremely low spin injection efficiency4,5. To maximize the potential of graphene for spintronic applications, various dielectric materials, such as metal oxides and van der Waals (vdW) hexagonal boron nitride (hBN)6–11, have been exploited and inserted between the FM electrode and graphene to form a tunnel contact in order to improve the injection efficiency12–14. In fact, the growth of a uniform oxide barrier is non-trivial and ubiquitous pinholes form due to high surface diffusivity on the dangling-bond-free graphene surface. By using TiO2 as a seed layer, an atomically smooth MgO barrier has been grown on graphene, so far with the widely accepted highest spin injection efficiency of 26–30%15. However, reaching such high efficiency relies on complex and delicate growth control based on ultra-high vacuum molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) technique, which hinders its widespread applications. Two-dimensional (2D) vdW hBN has been predicted as an ideal pinhole-free tunnel barrier16. Nevertheless, the precise control of its layer thickness and avoidance of transfer-process-induced contamination and bubbles/wrinkles are challenging, making the reported efficiency vary widely from device to device17–21.

A promising way to achieve reliable spin injection with simple processing is based on dielectric-barrier-free vdW contact between FM electrode and graphene, where naturally formed vdW gap serves as the tunnel barrier22,23. Recent studies using transfer techniques to stack 2D ferromagnet on graphene to form vdW contacts have claimed successful spin injection, but most without the explicit proof of Hanle precession signal24–27. Moreover, the efficiency remains low and scalability has yet to be addressed, as large-scale growth and transfer of 2D ferromagnets are immature. To advance toward scalable applications, making vdW contact based on three-dimensional (3D) FM metal instead of 2D ferromagnet is more promising28,29. Yet, directly evaporating 3D FM metal on 2D materials hardly forms vdW contact. Theoretical calculations have shown that FM metal, such as cobalt (Co), generates a strongly hybridized chemisorption interface when adsorbed on graphene, being the reason for forming a transparent contact with a negligible barrier and extremely small contact resistance30,31. A viable solution is to insert a buffer metal layer, which forms a physisorption interface with graphene, before depositing the FM metal layer so as to mitigate their direct hybridization. Inspiring results have been shown32,33, whereas, unambiguous demonstration of room-temperature spin injection via combinational observation of nonlocal spin valve signal and Hanle spin precession as well as achieving high spin injection efficiency, has yet to be realized.

In this work, by growing an indium (In) buffer layer between ferromagnetic Co electrode and graphene, we show that vdW contact with a gap of ~2.83 Å and an effective tunnel barrier height of ~62.8 meV has been successfully established. Analysis based on a one-dimensional drift-diffusion model of spin transport further corroborates the vdW-gap-mediated efficient spin tunnelling and transport in our Co/In-contacted devices. Both the nonlocal spin valve signal and Hanle spin precession have been explicitly observed at room temperature, which unambiguously proves successful spin injection via the vdW tunnel contact. Upon optimizing the In buffer layer thickness and gate control, a spin injection efficiency of ~25% at room temperature and ~35% at low temperature has been achieved, comparable to the best values reported in oxide-tunnel-barrier-based graphene lateral spin vales (LSV). By making a multi-channel LSV device on an ultra-long graphene sample, both high device yield and performance uniformity were demonstrated, further supporting the scalability of our approach. Finally, we show that our strategy is readily applicable to other 2D materials such as semiconducting MoS2, where an efficiency as high as ~19.7% was obtained.
